newsitem.title: UK: UK'S Clarke says Conservatives were unelectable.
newsitem.headline: UK'S Clarke says Conservatives were unelectable.

text.p: Former British finance minister Kenneth Clarke said on Sunday no one could have led his Conservative party to victory in the May 1 election which swept the Labour party into power and ousted prime minister John Major.
Laying out his stall for Tuesday's second round ballot for the leadership of what is now Britain's main opposition party, Clarke said defeat had been inevitable.

"Before the last election...the big issue was, was the Conservative party really still capable of being the natural governing party of this country," he told interviewer David Frost on national BBC television.

"I think if John Major was asking for sympathy it would be possible to look back and say look, probably the party wasn't leadable by anybody in its then state, John, and it probably wasn't electable."

Labour's landslide victory left just 164 Conservative members of parliament -- less than half the number the party had in the previous election -- to face a rejuvenated Labour party enjoying power for the first time in almost 19 years.
The 164 must this week select the man to replace Major, who announced after the election result that he was stepping down.

Clarke topped the first round ballot last Tuesday and polls show he is far and away the most popular candidate among rank and file Conservative members. But rank and file members, much to their anger, have no say in the choice of the party leader.
Former Welsh Secretary William Hague -- who told Frost he would "give it (the party) a shaking the like of which it has not had for a very long time if I win" -- is tipped as favourite.
Both Clarke and Hague, the youngest contender at just 36, promised on Sunday to include all wings of the party in their team if they won Tuesday's ballot.
But the third contender, former cabinet minister John Redwood, repeated calls for a tougher line on Europe.
Clarke warned that continuing to harp on about Europe would leave the party as split as it was before the May 1 election.

To win next Tuesday, a candidate needs the votes of more than half of the 164 Conservative MPs. If there is no winner, the first and second-placed candidates slug it out in a final ballot on Thursday.
